assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect revealed a genuinely new class of quantum matter, defined by topology and protected edge or surface states, and reshaped how condensed-matter physics classifies electronic phases. It is a rare case where theory predicted a state and experiment then realised it, and electronic-structure theory (band inversion, spin-orbit coupling) now routinely predicts topological materials. This is the kind of verified, surprising quantum behaviour in materials I find most compelling.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the decisive theoretical formulation of the Z2 quantum spin Hall insulator, and Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. This forms a clean theory-plus-experiment prize. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Hasan and others), are outside the supplied credit, so some allocation is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independent confirmations across HgTe, InAs/GaSb and many 3D materials with ARPES and transport, now almost two decades old, with broad impact on spintronics and topological quantum computing ideas. Timing is right and the 2016 topological-phase prize leaves room for this specific discovery.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions; the committee must be satisfied that the quantum spin Hall effect is distinct enough.
Whether the credit should include Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang cannot be resolved from the supplied names.
I recall the HgTe experiment but have not independently verified the details of the priority sequence.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a tunable platform for strongly correlated physics, with flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a carbon-only system. The theoretical prediction of flat bands at the magic angle followed by experimental observation is striking, and it is a vivid example of quantum mechanics still surprising us, in the spirit of graphene itself.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive continuum-model prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the key experimental discovery with the first author Yuan Cao, who is not in the credited list. Among the supplied names, MacDonald with Jarillo-Herrero is the cleanest pairing, with Bistritzer a possible third. The omission of Cao and of other contributors (the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto theory, and Dean, Kim and Young work on moire systems) is an allocation problem.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally reproduced by many groups, and the physics has grown into a large moire field, but the nature of the superconductivity and correlated states is still debated and theory cannot yet quantitatively explain them. This is somewhat young for a prize, though the field's momentum is very strong.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity and correlated insulators is unsettled.
Sample-to-sample variability and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility.
Credit boundaries, especially omitted experimentalist co-authors, are unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Car-Parrinello method unified density-functional theory with molecular dynamics, allowing first-principles simulation of bonding changes, liquids, defects and surfaces. Its originality and its lasting influence across physics, chemistry and materials science are very large, and it underpins much of modern computational materials theory. As a DFT practitioner I regard this as exceptionally foundational, though I must acknowledge a possible bias toward my own area.
assessment.attribution: Credit is compact and clear: the 1985 paper by Car and Parrinello. Two laureates are natural. Later developments by others (Born-Oppenheimer variants, Payne et al., plane-wave codes) are not needed to support a fair prize.
assessment.maturity: Four decades of use and independent implementation in many codes, with its reproducibility checked against other methods. Recognition is long overdue rather than premature, though the Nobel Committee has historically favoured a physical discovery over a method and the 1998 chemistry prize for DFT already recognised the underlying theory.
uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat a computational method as a physics discovery or invention within the will of Nobel.
The earlier chemistry prize (1998) for density-functional theory and computational chemistry may reduce appetite for a second computational prize.
I have a possible conflict of perspective as a computational materials theorist.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model and quantum phase transitions in a clean, tunable setting, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition as a landmark. It gives direct access to many-body physics that is hard to calculate, and complements electronic-structure theory by testing models of strongly correlated electrons.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac, Gardiner) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch observed the Mott transition; Esslinger realised fermionic Hubbard physics. Four names are credited but at most three can be selected, so someone important (Greiner or Bloch's early collaborators) is left out. I propose Bloch, Esslinger and Zoller as a balanced theory plus experiment configuration, but the choice is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with extensive independent confirmation across many laboratories and quantum gas microscopes. Recognition is timely, though 2001 BEC and 2012 prizes for atom control were adjacent.
uncertainties: Choice of three among four credited people is a difficult trade-off; Greiner and Jaksch are especially hard to exclude.
How much of the programme is a simulator for models versus a discovery about real materials remains a debated matter.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics created strong light-matter coupling with superconducting artificial atoms in microwave resonators, and is the architecture behind much of superconducting quantum information processing and quantum-limited readout. It is both a conceptual advance and technologically enabling.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal; Wallraff and colleagues made the first experiment. The supplied credit omits Wallraff, which weakens a fair configuration. Schoelkopf, Girvin and Blais is plausible among the supplied names but is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and widely adopted, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is very recent and closely related, so timing for another circuit prize is questionable.
uncertainties: Missing experimental credit (Wallraff) creates a real attribution gap.
Close proximity to the 2025 prize may crowd out this topic for some years.
Boundary between physics discovery and quantum-engineering platform is not sharp.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with the magic-wavelength idea, enabled fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and opened tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefinition of the second. It is a clear invention with quantifiable performance and wide impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock and Ye led its realisation to record precision, with a supplied two-person credit that appears coherent. Other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom) and the ion-clock and frequency-comb community are outside the credit, but the core configuration is defensible.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by multiple independent laboratories, with ongoing improvements; a redefinition of the second is pending. Hänsch and Hall already received the 2005 prize for the frequency comb, and Wineland the 2012 prize for ion control, which may reduce novelty.
uncertainties: Appetite for another precision-metrology prize after 2005 and 2012.
Whether Ye's role should be weighed alongside comb contributions already honoured in 2005.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of iron-based high-temperature superconductors opened a second family of high-Tc materials after the cuprates, with unconventional pairing in multiband magnetic systems. It was a real surprise, since iron and magnetism were thought hostile to superconductivity. Electronic-structure and spin-fluctuation theory has contributed to the understanding of these materials.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's group reported superconductivity in LaFeAsO(1-x)Fx in 2008, and Chen and Zhao's groups quickly raised Tc in related compounds. Hosono is the clear originator, while credit for Chen and Zhao is more about rapid follow-up and is a fair question.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced worldwide within weeks and now more than fifteen years old, but the pairing mechanism is not settled, and the Tc record in these materials is far below that of cuprates, which may limit the prize's appeal.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism remains debated, so the interpretation is not fully stable.
Whether Chen and Zhao's contributions are decisive or incremental.
The cuprate prize in 1987 may reduce the sense of novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Intrinsic long-range magnetic order in atomically thin van der Waals crystals (CrI3, Cr2Ge2Te6) shows that magnetism survives down to the monolayer, challenging expectations from the Mermin-Wagner theorem when anisotropy is present, and creating a platform for two-dimensional spintronics and heterostructure magnetism. It is close to my own research on 2D magnets and echoes the lesson of graphene.
assessment.attribution: Gong et al. (Zhang group, Cr2Ge2Te6) and Huang et al. (Xu group, CrI3) reported the decisive 2017 experiments. Jarillo-Herrero is credited here but his role is more in the later correlated-moire work, so I leave him out. Theoretical inputs and bulk precursors are not in the credit.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced across many groups, but the field is less than a decade old and the application path and theory of the magnetic anisotropy and exchange are still developing, so recognition is somewhat early.
uncertainties: Possibly premature relative to older candidates.
Credit overlap with other two-dimensional materials prizes and unresolved role of theorists.
Magnetic properties vary with layer number and substrate, so quantitative comparison to theory is still incomplete.
